utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Particularly today because there are people hiding behind poles, I would like to have appearances, please, for the both parties starting with Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Barney Thomas, Lorna Bolton, Salvatore Cannata, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thomas. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and to all in the courtroom. Daniela Tasic, Nikki Sethi, Tina Drolec, Milos Androvic, Eric Tully, Chad Mair, Novak Lukic, and I'm Gregor Guy-Smith for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I think I may have mispronounced one of the intern's names, but I'll take care of it at a later point in time and I do apologise to Nikki.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not a problem. Thank you very much. Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Martin Bell, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you may be seated. Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, can you begin, please, by giving us your full name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: My full name is Martin Bell and I was born on the 31st of August, 1938.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I'm a goodwill ambassador for UNICEF and a writer and a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Did you spend the large part of your career as a war correspondent employed by the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, from about 1966 to 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Could you just very briefly describe for Their Honours, the conflicts which you covered during that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It started with the Nigerian civil war, the Middle East wars in 1967 and 1973, the Vietnam war, wars in El Salvador and Nicaragua, the first Gulf war, and the wars of ex-Yugoslavia, chiefly in Croatia and in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: In 1997, what did you do after leaving the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: In 1997, I accidently fell into politics and I became for four years a member of the House of Commons.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That was as an independent MP?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I was the -- I was the first independent elected since 1951.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: During the course of your career did you receive any formal awards for journalism or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Oh, bits and pieces, yes. But they don't really mean very much to me, and one even from the queen. But you know, I think my chief benefit was experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The award you received from the queen was an OBE, Order of the British Empire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I think I got it for being the reporter most shot at in 1993 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: What does your current work with UNICEF involve?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: UNICEF have a variety of real celebrities which they can't send to war zones and so they send me because I'm -- I should be able to look after myself in these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And what is your function?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: As a witness, as a fundraiser, as someone who gives encouragement to their staff, locally and nationally, and someone who raises the profile of these issues at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And to again just briefly for the Trial Chamber's information, could you just tell us, please, what sort of areas, what sort of situations you've been sent to in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Some have been non-war zones, like Malawi, but they're are mostly scenes of conflict or recent scenes of conflict, Afghanistan, Darfur, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, places -- places like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, plainly you have acquired a lot of knowledge over the years about many different conflicts, but this afternoon I want to focus on your time in Sarajevo. Can you tell us when you first went to Sarajevo in the context of the conflict in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I first went to Sarajevo in March of 1992 at the -- on the occasion of the referendum on independence, and then when the war started in the first week in April, I went back and I stayed there on and off for much of the next three and a half years. Not just in Sarajevo, but in central Bosnia, in Mostar, in Tuzla, all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And what were you doing in Sarajevo during that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was the main reporter for BBC television there throughout the early months of the war, from April 1992 until I was wounded at the end of August 1992. I went back in rather reluctantly at the end of 1992 and worked a great deal in 1993 on the side war between Muslims and Croats in central Bosnia, but by March 1994, after the cease-fire between them, I returned to Sarajevo and spent much of the rest of the war there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: During the period between the end of 1992 when you were wounded, and when you say you returned to Sarajevo in March of 1994, did you spend time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did, even when I was based in Vitez and Gornji Vakuf. I used to make day trips or longer trips to Pale. I spent a lot of time with the Serbs. I had a reputation among the Sarajevo press corps, I suppose, of being pro-Serb. I wasn't, I was neutral and I had a very good friend who was one of the defenders of the Serb-held suburb of Grbavica and I used to go and see him. And one of the points that I would make is that there was no monopoly of suffering in this particular war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: From March 1994 onwards until the end of the war in Bosnia with the signing of the Dayton Accords, where were you largely based?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was based, I suppose, at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo for much of that time. Towards the end, I was based in Gornji Vakuf because the implementation of the Dayton Accords was done largely in the south of the country by British troops and they were -- in December 1995 they became -- they took off the blue helmets and they became NATO troops, and they broke through the former frontlines and implemented the agreement. So I was with them on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: During the -- during the period of between March 1994 until the end of the war, were you covering also other parts of Bosnia, were you travelling out of Sarajevo to cover any other parts of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There were -- it was increasingly hard by then to get the attention of my editors to what they perceived as a long-running war so they were losing interest in it. But I did quite a lot in northern Bosnia, in central Bosnia, but in Sarajevo itself, the fighting was especially intense in the summer of 1995. There were attempts, if you remember, there was the -- there was the kidnapping of UN troops in Pale, this was in May of that year. There was an attempt, there was a very strong attempt by the BiH, the Bosnian army, to break out of the encirclement in June. So I was in Sarajevo and reported those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I want to go back now to the situation in Sarajevo in 1992. In terms of your first arrival there and the outbreak of war in April 1992, what did that do to the city? What did that do to the civilians and the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was a little bit as if the Great War were being refought in a modern urban environment. And so many people were trapped in these high-rise buildings. I mean trapped in the sense there was no electricity so the lifts didn't work, the winter of 1992 to 1993 was a very bitter winter. A lot of the -- there was no water-supply so the only water they could get either out of the river or from standpipes which were themselves under fire. I mean, I think looking back it was a truly desperate time for all of the people on Sarajevo, I would say, on both side of the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: By that time, the winter of 1992/1993, were the confrontation lines in Sarajevo reasonably firmly established?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, they were. I would say they probably -- there was a tremendous battle in Sarajevo, I think, on the 22nd of May, 1992, and after that the confrontation lines changed very, very little until November/December 1995. Occasionally a trench line would be lost, a group of houses would change hands, but you know, I think if you looked at the map in the end of 1995, it's roughly where the frontlines were established in the early summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If I were to show you a map, would you feel comfortable providing us with some general indication as to where the confrontation lines were?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could please have Exhibit P 439 on the screen, which is map number 8 in the court binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, just while that's appearing on the screen, you've testified previously in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Firstly as a witness for the Defence in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And more recently as a Prosecution witness in the Dragomir Milosevic case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I think they were using this technology in the Dragomir Milosevic case. You can see that we have an image on the screen. The image can be blown up and manipulated without altering the image in various different ways. You will recognise the image as a map of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: For the purposes of marking the confrontation lines, do you need a closer view?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I would like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Is that sufficient or too close?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. What I'm going to do is ask Mr. Usher if he can provide you with a means to electronically mark the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And what we are looking for, Mr. Bell, is as best you can to simply mark the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I hope I'm looking in the right direction, but you will notice that right in the middle on what we call the Bridge of Brotherhood and Unity, the Serbian lines came right down to there, so it was not a case of Serbs on the hills around and the Bosnian government forces trapped inside. They came right down there and the suburbs of Ilidza and Grbavica were both in the Serbian hands right through to the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If we can just pause for a moment there. First of all, can you using the marker circle the Bridge of Brotherhood and Unity which you have just --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I don't have a clear enough view. I need it -- need to be closer than I see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll leave that for a moment. Can you circle the areas of Ilidza and Grbavica that you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yeah. Ilidza was at one end of the airport runway.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If you could just mark that with an I.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Grbavica I'm having difficulty with because I'm going too far back but I would guess it would be around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, would it help if we got in closer?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It might do. It's a rather -- it's a very detailed map.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't intend to tender this version of the map. If we could go into just a little closer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why don't you want to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Because I'll get the markings done on a clearer version of the map by Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Again, if we start with the Bridge of Brotherhood and Unity, can you see it on the map there this time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The bridges are not very clearly marked, but I would guess it's probably around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could just mark that with a B.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can you just mark that with the letter B, Mr. Bell? Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you mark with a circle the area of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it was around about -- it's this end of the runway.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Mark that with the letter I, please.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It's the left-hand marking that we see on the map?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think the key thing is that the Serbs were at both ends of the runway. Ilidza there and Lukavica barracks at the other end, I'll just mark that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: And the government forces were on either side including this, I'll mark it here, this is Dobrinja. I'll mark it with a D. That was the old press village in the winter Olympics and the other side of it is the village of Butmir, which I'll mark with a B. So you have the government forces at both sides of the runway and the Serb forces at both ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, when you are talking about the government forces you are talking about the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. We have great difficulty with the terminology because they had some Serbs fighting for them as well, what they called the loyal Serbs, but I would normally call them Bosnian government forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If we could tender that, please, as a Prosecution exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Its admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P514.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'd like to go again, please, to the blank map, P 439.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, if you could draw on this map what you were about to draw for me a few minutes ago, which was the confrontation line, please. And if you need to go in closer, please say so.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: This will be actually quite difficult to do. It was something like, like down here and out and a much bigger range around. I mean, this is a highly inaccurate but it would be something of that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Just a couple of questions about that. The area that you've marked as being held by the Serbs, Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do we see that on the map there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it's roughly this end of the -- this end of the -- of the runway. I've probably drawn the -- I probably put the line too not sufficiently. That I will amend because actually it came quite close to the end of the runway.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. There is a means of erasing the line if you need to use that, please say so and Mr. Usher will help you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, I think I've corrected it, that should suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is erase the redundant part of that line so that when we look at this map in several months' time, it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can you help by erasing, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you will please connect the correct line now, Mr. Bell. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do we see on that map the area of Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it was the -- it was beyond -- I mean, it's such small print but it was really beyond Butmir on the -- on the sort of southern edge of that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Was that within the confrontation lines or --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was -- it was -- it was -- I wouldn't say it was a frontline village but it came under -- under bombardment especially in 1995 with -- with rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The area within the line that you have drawn was occupied by the forces of which army?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: There were -- within they were the forces of the Bosnian government, BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just, if you don't mind just righting ABiH in there, please.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And presumably on the other side of the line?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: On the other side of the line were the forces of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Known as the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Known as the VRS. I'll fill that in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And can you circle for us the area of Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I'm doing this from memory because I can't see it. But I -- it's roughly towards the bottom of Mount Igman there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Would you mark that with an H, please?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And Hrasnica was held by the forces of which army?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was held actually by the forces of the BiH, in which case I obviously again have to reconnect this line. I'm going to have to -- it was more like that because both Butmir and Hrasnica were held by the -- by the Bosnian government forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Again with Mr. Usher's assistance, if you would just remove the redundant line, please.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I have to apologise for this, it's a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: We all understand, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I could please tender that map as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P515.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, you've explained that these lines change little from the time when you first arrived in Sarajevo until the end of the war. What did the position or the shape of these lines mean for the population which occupied that part within the lines of encirclement, the civilians in the area marked ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Mostly they were overlooked by high ground, especially, I would say, on the south side of the city, and they would then be within line of sight of snipers in some areas; but at the same time, the -- Grbavica, for instance, was in line of sight of snipers from the other side operating out of the old parliament office building and vantage points like that. So there was no -- I mean, I don't think anyone lived safely in that city at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Was there an easy means of entry into and exit from the city for the civilians in ABiH-held territory?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: There was no easy means at all. There was in the latter half of the war a tunnel constructed underneath the airport runway which provided a means of reinforcement and supplies to come into the city. But for any -- anyone who wanted to leave, unless they had the right permissions and the right influence, I mean, they were more or less, they had to endure the whole siege. We were in a different state because we had United Nations passes and we were able with difficulty to come through Bosnian Serb roadblocks in Ilidza and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You mentioned the high ground being occupied by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: What I want to refer you to now is map or photograph number 10 in the booklets, Your Honour, which is 65 ter number 09242.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, do you recognise that as an aerial photograph of Sarajevo and its surrounds?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You've spoken of the airport and is that what we see in the bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I firstly tender the unmarked photograph as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it not already been tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, Your Honour. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P516.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the confrontation lines that you drew for us on the other map and your comment about the VRS holding the high ground, can you point out again with the pointer, mark the areas of high ground that were held by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think there is one area in particular which I shall ... If I can, this area here is high ground that they held with a commanding view of some of the streets below.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Were there any areas of high ground held to the north of the city?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: This -- the high ground I shall mark now, again it's approximate, had on it the television transmitter and was actually used as a training-ground by the BiH Army for awhile. The lines of conflict are further north, were further out than that, so you are talking about the high ground commanding the city centre, it's the area that I've outlined on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. If you could just mark that right-hand circle, please, with VRS.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: One question, actually, Mr. Bell, before we leave that photograph, do we see on the area of the photograph where this tunnel was that you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It would be roughly, I can sort of put it in here. I never took it myself because I went around it because the entrances were often under mortar fire, but it was roughly on the line that I've given there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, if I could please tender the marked photograph as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before we do that, could we have a marking of some sort, either a BiH indicating the training grounds or T for the television transmitter so that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I put T or BiH because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Whatever. Whatever works because otherwise months from now we won't have an indication of what that is either.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: No problem with that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have thought if we've got VRS written on the right-hand side, we probably might write ABiH on the left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course in both cases it's not the only place they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I'm just marking high ground on either side of the city centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Quite understood. Maybe put a T on the tunnel, next to the tunnel. Then the map as marked is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P517.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, Madam Registrar. Your Honours, I wonder if we could have, I'm not sure if it's possible to do this on the same screen, but photograph number 12 from the booklet which is 65 ter number 09241.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Maybe we can start with that image, Mr. Bell --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Which, Your Honours, is the page marked "left" in photograph 12 of the booklets that Your Honours have, and is the left-hand half of Exhibit 65 ter 09241.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You spoke of a tower -- a hill with a television tower on it. Is that what we see in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's what you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And has the photograph been taken from the high ground that you marked as occupied by the VRS in the previous photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It could have been taken from there, but it might possibly have been taken from the Olympic village which was on ground held by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If we -- can we scroll to the right, Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: By scrolling to the right, does that assist you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it does. And by scrolling to the right, I would say it was more likely taken from the old Olympic village because the high ground overlooking the city centre was to the right. You see the yellow Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: What we call the Sniper's Corner would be about, oh, 400 yards to the right of that. And that was overlooked by high ground controlled by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And that was, as we look at the photograph, off to the right-hand side of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Would the vantage or the view from the VRS positions bear any resemblance to the sort of view that we see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: A marginal resemblance, but in fact they were -- they were closer. They were looking down the -- latterly down the side-streets. You'll see there was a hill beyond the Holiday Inn. I used to camp out there with my camera in July 1995. It was a dangerous place but an excellent vantage point; we called it Gypsy Hill. So in fact, I would have said that the VRS soldiers, if they were so minded, would have actually had a clearer view than the one taken from this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, could we tender this photograph, please, as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P518.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, you've spoken of the Holiday Inn which we see is the yellow building in the middle of the photograph as it appears on the screen at the moment. And is that where you were stationed for a time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. Not at the very start of the war because it was damaged in the early days, but from about June 1992 I stayed there on and off because I was away in central Bosnia a lot. I stayed there, really, until the end of the war. It was the main press headquarters even though one side of it was uninhabitable because it was damaged by shell fire and other fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Which side was uninhabitable?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: What you see -- it would be the right side. The side roughly facing the tall building beside it which is the parliament office building.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. And that was as a result of fire from which forces?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That would be as a result of fire from the Bosnian Serb-held side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. So that we can now begin to orientate ourselves relative to the map that we have already viewed, I'd like to go back, please, to Exhibit P439. And if we could close-up, please, on the main part of the city. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, are you able to mark on the map, as it presently appears on the screen, the location of the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I would imagine, though it's a very indistinct map to me, it's about there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If you could just mark that with an H, please?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could please tender that as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P519.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned, Mr. Bell, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. We don't need your help anymore. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. Bell, the plight of civilians in the ABiH-held territory, and the sniping and shelling. Can you please tell us, first of all, what the situation in that respect was like at the end of 1992, beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, this was a war fought, looking at it from my perspective, against all the Geneva Conventions. There was no distinction between military and civilian targets, except of course that the civilians were not able to defend themselves. They had to come out for food and water and fuel if they could gather it and many of them spent, especially the children spent much of those three and a half years in cellars.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: What would happen to civilian who were outside?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I had an experience in -- I was doing a report in early 1993 and we discovered there was a water point, a stand pipe, a tap which people had to come out to within range of the Bosnian Serb positions and people were regularly shot as they fetched their water. Sometimes the trams were targeted in a similar way. There was -- to me one of the iconic images of the war - and this was towards the end - is a French armoured personnel carrier shuttling roughly between the parliament office building and what we knew as Sniper's Corner, and for once UNPROFOR, the UN Protection Force was doing some protecting and they -- the civilians would walk with the -- the armoured personnel carrier went at walking pace and it would protect the civilians who were obviously sheltered on the safer side of it. I mean, I've never seen -- I've never been in a war quite so merciless as this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You've spoken of the effect in terms of trams, in terms of needing to fetch water. What were the -- besides the effects of sniping and shelling directly, what did this do to day-to-day life in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, it -- it really closed down. The business -- people's only business - and this applies to both sides of the lines - was survival, just getting through -- getting through the day. Especially difficult in the winter because it's a very cold winter there. There was -- there were no -- the gas was turned off for most of the time. There was no electricity. There was no source of food apart from what the United Nations could bring in. So the people really, really suffered on -- to an extent that I hadn't seen in all my other wars, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: How frequent were the -- and again, focusing on the period the end of 1992, beginning of 1993 for a moment, how frequently were civilians getting shot and civilians getting shelled by the VRS forces?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: This was not something that happened at a steady rate over three and a half years. Apart from the first winter of the war, 1992 to 1993, which was particularly grim, there would be in the early months of the year, I think January, February, middle of March, something of a cease-fire and this is when there were actually cease-fire negotiations. But when the snow and the ice melted about the middle of March, you would find that the pace of the shelling and the fighting quickened and there was a lot of, I mean, there were some -- there were main force engagements like the attempt by the BiH Army to break the siege of Sarajevo in June/July 1995. So it was almost a seasonal thing and I would say that some times were much worse than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Were you in any position to assess whether or not civilians were specifically targeted?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Common sense says yes. I remember a cameraman in the Holiday Inn just sort of zeroing his camera one morning, poking it out of the window to make sure that it worked and there was an old lady getting out of a van and going into a house, so he just -- he was just making sure and as he did so she was shot. I think it's highly unlikely that she was shot by accident. It would seem -- common sense would say she was targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Were there areas of the city which were more prone to attacks on civilians than others?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking those areas where the snipers and the gunners on the VRS side of the lines would have a clear line of sight down one of the side-streets. You understand that the main street goes from one end to the other, but the side-streets were especially vulnerable and this is where the notorious Sniper's Corner was, and they actually had a road sign saying, "Beware snipers," which was up for three and a half years. But of course, having said that you were vulnerable to mortar fire wherever you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Was that vulnerability to mortar fire consistent throughout the three and a half year?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, I don't think the level of fighting was consistent throughout the three and a half years. I would say it was at its worst in the summer of 1992 and again in that resurgence of the fighting in summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: What were the respective strengths and weaknesses in terms of weaponry and manpower of the two forces?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The Serbs obviously had the advantage in heavy weapons, in armoured personnel carriers, in tanks, they even had a tank in the suburb of Grbavica. In bombs and rockets. The BiH Army, although it was much more lightly equipped, had the advantage in numbers. Numerical superiority. The Serbs by about the fourth -- third year of the war were seriously defeated -- depleted. They had, I mean every -- this was a citizens army. Everyone who could bear arms did bear arms, but the main units of the Romanija Corps, the corps that surrounded Sarajevo, were seriously under strength, lacking officers, lacking sufficient NCOs. And even though when we were -- we could -- I had very good relations with the Serbs right up to August 1994 and I would -- and Karadzic and others would sometimes take us around their frontlines and show us the spirit of these soldiers. I mean, it was all part of what we call the information campaign, but I noticed up there there were a lot of very old men, and I raised this with Jovan Zametica who was a Cambridge don who was his foreign policy advisor whom I knew very well. I said, Jovan, you know, you are going to lose, why don't you deal, and he said - I'll never forget this - he said, We don't care. So there was an imbalance between the two forces. The heavy weapons on one side, but the manpower on the other. And of course, towards the end of the war, the Bosnian government forces found ways of getting more weaponry, especially anti-tank weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: So how did this imbalance manifest itself in the military exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It manifested itself in a growing ability of the Bosnian army seriously to threaten the Serbs' stranglehold on the city. About June 1995, we had some amazing images where they actually broke out for awhile and over the old Pale road. They had -- they tried to break the siege from the outside, but suffered very severe casualties. So what you got towards the end of the war which you hadn't really had so much before was exchanges of fire between main force units on either side, which didn't make the civilians any safer, but there were times when it was a war of one army against another.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: So what would the response of the VRS be?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, I noted that what would happen, and the government forces were, I mean, I remember reflecting at one time that Harry Silajdzic who was a senior member of the presidency, I felt he had the effect of a whole brigade of marines or something, because he could -- what would happen was that the government forces might snipe or make some aggressive move to try and break the siege and then they would really get hit very, very hard with artillery, with tank fire, you could see this in the early months of the war. So then the -- Silajdzic would turn around and say, Look what are they doing to us, we are the victims, why will the world not move to save us? And you had this especially in 1995 with the use of aircraft bombs powered by rockets and indeed by the use of phosphorus which was also used then.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I want to ask you a little bit about these bombs that you've just described. Which forces used these aircraft bombs propelled by rockets?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Any force would use whatever it had. And the Bosnian army actually had very little in terms of heavy weapons. When the Croats were besieging Gornji Vakuf in the side war in 1993 to 1994, they were actually rolling sea mines down hills into the village. You used whatever you had. Now, by then there was a no-fly zone in force and the government, the Serb side had these aircraft bombs that it couldn't use because it couldn't use its aircraft so it devised a means of getting them propelled by rockets. There was, while was there I think there was three of these cases, one was in Vlasenica, one was in the bus depot which was a UN vehicle compound opposite the television station, and one of course was actually in the well of the television station itself, which did great damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can you describe what you know of the effect of these bombs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I only came in after they had been fired and these were, I believe, 500-pound aircraft bombs and they were completely devastating. They were the heaviest weapons used, I mean, relative to the tank and artillery shells used from the early days of the war, these were the heaviest weapons that were employed throughout the whole course of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The ones which you saw or the sites that you went to, were they at military installations or were they in civilian areas?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Hrasnica I didn't see because I couldn't get there. The UN compound was a UN compound. It was a former bus depot so by definition it had no military -- no competent military inside it, and the television station was also a civilian installation by definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Besides the buildings themselves, were the immediate surrounding areas civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I know of no military installations anywhere near the television station and the bus compound opposite it. The principal army headquarters were down-town; and the other military areas, if you like, were on the -- on the frontlines. But not around those target zones, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Generally speaking, where were the -- geographically, where were the ABiH troops deployed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: They were deployed obviously round the, round the edges. They were -- they would -- you would sometimes find them billeted in schools, but you were not aware of a -- living in a city with a great mass with a standing army in it. This was a war fought very piecemeal, house by house and sector by sector. And apart from when I -- we did a story about the Bosnian government forces training on that hill near the television tower, that is the one time I've seen them en masse, apart from the attempt to break the encirclement in June 1992 where they were moving very rapidly up hill and under covering fire, but it looked like a ruined city, but I would say not a militarised [Realtime transcript read in error "mill tear terrorised"] one in any obvious way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: When you talk about the troops being deployed around the edges, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Could you mind if I just correct something. There's -- that word should be militarised, not "mill tear terrorised," three lines up. I'm not accusing anyone of being a terrorist here. Sorry. That's right. Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bell, when you mentioned the troops, the ABiH troops being deployed around the edges, what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I'm talking about the frontlines, sir. This was a war in which, you know, the frontlines could be as little as 30 metres from each other. It was house to house, and very often there would be a kind of a local cease-fire either explicit or just agreed between commanders, but there were -- but every inch of ground was fought for from, oh, I'd say May 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You spoke earlier, Mr. Bell, of the gas being turned off, the electricity being turned off, and you've described people having to go to certain collection points for water. Why would that be?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The gas came into Sarajevo from outside. The water was on a main. The one consistent source of water throughout, of course, was the Miljacka River, and you would find people in the middle of winter drawing their water from it, carrying it in handcarts, in any way, because you can -- you know, these people had to come out to get their water. It was one of the effects of fighting a war, I would say an early 20th century war in a late 20th century urban environment. This is why the war, terrible as it was, out in the -- out in the country-side was not -- did not have as severe an effect as the war in the cities. Not just Sarajevo, but Mostar and Tuzla as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: When you were in Sarajevo the first time, late 1992, early 1993, what were you reporting?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was reporting initially the result of the referendum campaign, and then I was reporting the start of the war, the street fighting in Sarajevo, the massive flight of refugees especially from Eastern Bosnia. We went up to Zvornik. We still had a degree of movement. I was reporting the politics of it. I spent a lot of time in Pale with Jovan Zametica, with Karadzic, with Nikola Koljevic, his vice-president. You know, we tried to be as comprehensive as we could in rather difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Did that reporting include what was happening to the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it did. It was -- it very much did. The report I did from outside Zvornik, we were watching, I think, 20.000 civilians on the move in that one day. And since civilians were the principal casualties of this war, a lot of the reporting was about their plight.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Including the reporting from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Including the reporting from Sarajevo. On both sides of the -- on both sides of the lines, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The -- at the time you were there, in late 1992, early 1993, how large was the international press contingent in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: There were about -- I wouldn't have thought that even at the height it was more than about 50. It was a very difficult place to get to. The costs of protection were high, the logistics were difficult, so those of us present throughout were actually relatively few, which, from my point of view, had the advantage that you could get to the main people. You could get to the UN generals, you could get to the Bosnian Serb leadership. It wasn't done through spin doctors and press officers. No, there were not that many of us and we bonded together pretty well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Was everybody interested in the same sort of stories that you have described?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: There was more of an agreed agenda than I think there is now. Yes, on the whole. There were no tabloid press there very much. I don't think there were any great differences between us in the way that we covered the story, except that I probably spent more time with the Serbs than most of the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: What sort of networks, press agencies, and other organisations were represented at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: There were the -- obviously Reuters was there, Associated Press was there, AFP was there, the BBC was there, CNN, and French television. But we put together a -- because it was so dangerous, I took the initiative and knocked some heads together and we actually formed what we called the Sarajevo Agency Pool so that the cameramen and women were not competing with each other to go into the most dangerous places, and I think we saved some lives with that. So it was an unusually close-knit and non-competitive group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And what was that group of people doing with its footage?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: They went -- those footage went out on satellite exchanges all over the world. I know that because the story that I sent from -- about the refugees being driven out of the villages around Zvornik, and Zvornik itself by a paramilitary leader called Zeljko Raznjatovic. Hisnom de guerre was Arkan, I knew him very well. He -- that -- we started off with some footage taken by a cameraman of mine in Zvornik of the dead Muslims being carried out and the Serbian flag hoisted, and whatever I said clearly offended this warlord and because it was seen in -- it was seen in Belgrade, and I had to backtrack in some way on my comments the next day to try and reduce the risk to him. His name was Dragan and he was seriously threatened. So yeah, these images went around Europe and we went around the world, especially in the early phases of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: When you returned in early 1994 and through to the end of the war, were the same sorts of stories being reported in the international press from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, I rather feel that a degree of war fatigue set in. At the same time, the -- what they call in the military field security tightened up a lot, so you couldn't just roll around everywhere with your armoured vehicle, you were stopped and blocked, and there was much more of an attempt to manipulate the press. But the images of -- from May 1995 through to the, really, through to Dayton, they were so graphic that they were going around the world as much as in that first summer of the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: During the period of March 1994 through to the end of the war, was there a constant international press presence in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was constant but I would have thought it waned, interest diminished to the news editors of Europe and the United States; it was a long war which had been going on a long time. You know, I was already competing with a change in the news agenda in which a royal divorce, for instance, is thought to be much more important than a European war. But that -- towards the end May, June, July 1995, that lack of interest had gone away and people really did want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Does that mean there was no coverage of what was happening to civilians during this time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, there was always coverage. The Sarajevo agency pool had two especially able Bosnian cameramen who got everywhere. We kept working, we kept working hard, and I found that by early summer of 1995 my own editors in London were waking up to the fact that this was the -- probably the climactic phase of the war. I think this really came home after the Srebrenica massacre of July 1995, it then became a war, shall we say, on the conscience of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Were you involved in reporting of the Srebrenica massacre?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Only from the outside. It was denied. It took really quite a few weeks and even months for the true reality to dawn. The first -- I mean, we knew these people had disappeared but we couldn't prove they had been killed, but there were some aerial photographs taken by the Americans which suggested so. I would think it was not really until about September 1995 that the -- you know, it was possible for people to deny this had happened. Well, after I suppose September 1995 it was no longer possible, and I think this contributed to the political initiative that ended the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can you tell me what Eurovision is?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Eurovision is a syndicate of all the European broadcasters. Besides its, you know, the song contest and all the other things, it's core is an exchange of news footage between its broadcasters and they all take in each others news feeds, or they did then, at a regular time every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Was it operating during 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it was. In fact, our initial satellite dish when we were based -- when we first got in in April 1995, we were based in the Hotel Srbija in Ilidza actually, in Serb-held territory, and our dish was a Eurovision dish. It was actually provided by the European broadcasting union, so the Eurovision was at the heart of this enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just in practical terms, what would happen to footage, what would Eurovision do with it, what would other subscribers do with the Eurovision footage?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Before we formed the Sarajevo agency pool, the main television news agencies, Reuters which was then called Viz News, and what was then WTN, World Television News, and APTN, which was -- they would -- they would offer up their images of the day and an adjudicator in Geneva would decide to take this agency's or that agency's. After we formed the Sarajevo agency pool in May 1992, there was this Eurovision rep, somebody on the ground who would scoop up everything that was available and send it at a given time to the European networks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Eurovision pool of material was regularly accessed by subscribers, did they download or retrieve footage on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, I used to get letters from all corners of Europe, so they obviously did. You have to understand, there was no -- apart from CNN, there was no rolling news at that time. But there were all the large and even the small European broadcasters, they showed intense interest. We had -- I mean, I could see that by the people coming through. We had Irish television, German television, French television, Austrians, I mean, everybody was there, and they were there because they had seen this on their screens and they wanted to send their own people and own correspondents. So it was -- I spent -- after Croatia, I think you have to understand this was the first war in Europe since 1945 so it would have been surprising if there had not been this interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Were there any Serb networks who or which subscribed to Eurovision, Republic of Serbia networks?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't in Belgrade at the time for obvious reason, but Yugoslav television was a member of the European broadcasting union in good standing and so obviously -- well, it certainly received what we sent or my cameramen wouldn't have been threatened whenever it was, it was in April 1992. And of course, there were, I mean, if you could consider the Serb's own interest in Bosnia, it would have been extraordinary if they turned their backs on it which they didn't. And of course we had quite a lot of Serbian journalists came in as well. The Associated Press correspondent was a Serb. A lot of the networks initially sent their reports -- of the agency sent their reports through Belgrade because they were still in the old Yugoslav system, so Serbian journalists were quite heavily involved, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just give me a moment, please, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all I have for Mr. Bell at the moment. I've just been handed a note which might suggest that there are one or two errors in the transcript which I'd want to have a look at in case they need any further clarification from Mr. Bell. I wonder if we could take the adjournment now and I can use that time to find those mistakes and see whether Mr. Bell is required to comment on those at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, then. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Yes, there are a couple of passages in the transcript which I'd like to refer back to Mr. Bell, please, Your Honours. The first is at page 27, line 12. And I wonder if we could have that passage appear on the screen before Mr. Bell, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You want me to fill in the gap?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Bell --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: You wish me to fill in the gap?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Let me just find where we are for a moment. Yes, you see the reference to 27:1 on the left-hand side? Do you --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If you scroll -- if you go down to the number 12?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that name is Jovan, J-o-v-a-n, Zametica, Z-a-m-e-t-i-c-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Nikola Koljevic, K-o-l-j-e-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And Your Honours, there's one more passage, please, page 31, line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And you were talking -- first of all, do you see the reference to 31:1?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And if you go down to line number 10 under there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: We were talking about Eurovision?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I've made -- I've maken [sic] a mistake there. It's April 1992, of course, when we first got in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bell, thank you. Those were the only matters I wanted to raise with you. My learned friends for the Defence will have some questions for you if you would kindly wait there for us, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Keep forward.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please use the other microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is this better?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you'll excuse me, Mr. Bell, I have a tendency to drop my voice and I get into trouble because they can't hear me and can't interpret then they yell at me, and I'd rather not have that happen too terribly much while we are talking to each other. I've had occasion to read all of your testimony in all of the cases previously and I've had occasion to read the book or one of the books that you've written, "In Harm's Way." And I think I'd like to start my examination based upon what I've seen previously as well as what I've seen today, echoing the remarks that were made by Judge Jorda in which he said: "I also thank you for the quality of your testimony to which you always try to take the high ground vis-a-vis this dreadful conflict." And in my discussions with you today, I'm really searching for that kind of a balance, because you are uniquely situated to comment on and give us some understanding of a number of, I think, very important issues that surround this particular litigation and this particular conflict. You said on your direct testimony that this war, unlike other wars that you had reported, was different. You mention at one point that it was a re-enactment or perhaps a Great War again, and you also mentioned that it was an early 20th-century war being fought late in the 20th century. And I'd like to start there for a moment, if I could. And could you explain to us what the distinctions that you believe existed in this war were based upon your experience for many years as a war correspondent in many theatres of operation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think I would start by saying I sometimes felt, especially in central Bosnia, that I had blundered into some scenes from 1914 to 1918. That is, the weapons used in Bosnian war were almost entirely, apart from the aircraft bombs, I suppose, the same weapons used in the Great War. They were assault weapon, they were mines, they were machine-guns, and so on. But the difference, I think, was that the extent to which in a late 20th century war in an urban environment civilians were so much caught up in it and it wasn't just that there was no distinction between the soldiers and the civilians. I sometimes felt the civilians were being targeted, and political leaders would use the sufferings of their people to advance their political cause. And the same thing happened in the war in Croatia. I think -- I think that's why I found this -- of the 18 wars that I have reported, I found this the most shocking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say that political leaders used the suffering of the people sometimes to advance their cause, earlier in your direct testimony, you had mentioned one of the things that occurred as a result of what would happen when the BiH would attempt to break out of an area and then they would be hit with this heavy response and there would be, then, a response from a gentleman whose name has just escaped me. I can't remember what his name was --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Oh, Silajdzic maybe?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Silajdzic, yes. In that regard, he, then, would go forth and say, See what they are doing to us. And I'm wondering, is that what you are talking about or is that an example of what you are referring to when you are talking about in one sense the political leadership using the suffering of their people to advance their cause?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, at the same time the political leadership would have been, from their own point of view, quite sincere. I remember Haris Silajdzic taking to task General Sir Michael Rose, who was UNPROFOR commander, in a very public way and attempting to humiliate him. I think I would like to make a distinction between main force unit clashes like the one I described when the BiH forces attempt to break the siege in the summer of 1995, and the day-to-day shelling and, as I see it, sniping of and targeting of civilians. I mean, this was a war with where both these things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In this war, do you find that the - I'm trying to figure out how to say this properly - that the status of the media was distinct from that of the other wars that you've reported? I'm trying -- and to be perfectly honest with you, I'm trying to edge up to, I think, where you know this discussion is going.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yeah. I'll be as helpful as I can. When the war began in April 1992, the international community as such was hardly on the ground. The UNPROFOR had its headquarters in Sarajevo when the war began, but they left hurriedly in May 1992. So as far as the international community was concerned, there were one or two European monitors, but as far as the peoples of Bosnia were concerned, the only representatives they saw of the international community were the international press. And therefore, there would be obviously an attempt to influence us, to get us to put their point of view and we understood this. So it was an unusual war in that respect as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That, I think, falls or flows into a comment that's often made, it's an old saw, and I certainly, from what I've seen, am not accusing you in this in any respect whatsoever, but the first casualty of a war is truth. And to the extent that that is something that is of concern, I think as a reporter it's clearly something that must have been to concern not only to you but of to your colleagues? That you made sure that you were both objective and telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And anything you do is fragmentary because you are concentrating on what you find at a particular time and a particular place. But especially in the early months of the war, we did have most remarkable access to both sides. And I'll be honest, that one of the -- one of the problems I had dealing with my editors, and they were not unique in this, was that they got themselves very early into a mindset of good Muslims and bad Serbs, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: And when an ambulance with Serbian soldiers was intercepted and hijacked and eight or nine Serbs were killed in cold blood, I had great difficulty impressing on my editors that this had actually happened. But I think, you know, obviously you ask yourself, What did I get wrong? I think I'd stand by just about everything I wrote and said at the time. Always accepting that it was necessarily fragmentary and I could only be where I was and not somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe, as you've commented, one of the things that is true about war is that war is in fact local?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: All wars are local, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All wars are local. As a matter of fact, that's a point that you raise in your book which is that what is going on on the ground at the time is in fact what is most pressing to all those that are involved in that issue?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It's the field where you fight, it's the ditch where you die.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you initially, if I'm not mistaken, you initially came to the area with regard to the referendum process?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Referendum, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'd like to, for a moment, see if what you said in your book still holds true, and that's with regard to the issue of what I would call the Genscher push, which I think you understand what I mean, to recognise the independence. And in your book you say, and this is on page 35, which I believe is pages 2 and 3 in e-court, you say: "The then Secretary-General of the United Nations Javier Perez de Cuellar, in the final days of a distinguished term of office" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- "wrote to the president of the council of ministers, Hans van den Broek of Holland, to convey the sense of foreboding expressed by Cyrus Vance after meeting many of the main players including the Bosnian leadership. More than one of his high-level interlocutors described the explosive consequences of such a development as being a potential time bomb ... and I'm deeply worried that an early selective recognition could widen the present conflict and fuel an explosive situation especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina and also Macedonia. I believe, therefore, that uncoordinated actions should be avoided." Lord Carrington wrote to a similar effect, I'm going to skip a couple of lines: "... an early recognition of Croatia would undoubtedly mean the break-up of the conference. There is also a real danger, perhaps even a probability that Bosnia-Herzegovina will also ask for independence and recognition which would be wholly unacceptable to the Serbs in the Republic. This might well be the spark that sets Bosnia-Herzegovina alight." Some years later after reflection, and I know it's in your book, do you still hold that same position?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I was passed all the documents relating to the debate on the recognition of Croatia and I think now looking back on it, it was an absolutely pivotal event, and all the predictions made by Carrington and others, they all sadly were proved true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you, during the time that you were in the region, discuss with Serbian leadership or Serbs at all the fact of the European decision to recognise these particular quests for self-determination and independence?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I almost certainly discussed it during -- in the margins of my reporting on the referendum campaign in March 1992, because by then the decisions on Croatia had been -- had been taken. And you will notice that, like all civil wars, the civil war in Bosnia -- well, it was more than a civil war, but it was partly a civil war. It was slow to start because the people of Bosnia had a very acute sense of what was going to happen once it started. So I almost certainly did discuss this with the Serb leadership, Karadzic and Koljevic especially. This is when I got to know them first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We may have a moment to speak about Mladic. I take it this is something that you did not speak with General Mladic about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, General Mladic was not in the frame at that time. He was a general in the JNA based elsewhere. I never knew him as well as the others because I was dealing with the political leadership, but I did at one time in August 1992, I prevented him -- I intervened to prevent him throttling the Reuters correspondent Kurt Schork, whom he'd taken against in a big way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you suggested that if the other side would control theirs then you would control yours, because Mladic was somewhat upset what with the Reuters correspondent was accusing him of; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is true, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What I'm trying to come to is an understanding because part of what we are dealing here -- with here is the issue of, in a very real way, perception of that which is being said. And I want to frame it in the following way, and if it's a fair characterization, tell me; and if it's not a fair characterization, tell me that too. You say at page 103 of your book, that's page 9 of the e-court, you say: "At the same time, and rather to my surprise, I found the Serbs quite easy to like on a personal and social level. Once they even sought to use me to pass a message to the British government, though I protested to them it was none of my business. They could be warm hearted and hospitable and even almost innocent in a," and this is what I'm driving at here," 14th-century kind of way, which is not to excuse them, but rather to suggest that they belong to a different age. Yet they were doing damage in this one and the problem was to get through to them." When I think of the 14th century, I think of the plague, the Hundred Years' War, it was a time when society was relatively shut down, and the people were unnecessarily isolated and concerned about information that came from the outside. And I'm wondering if that is a fair characterization of your experience with the Serbs, and if that's what you meant with regard to that particular language?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I refer to the 14th century because I had in mind the battle of Kosovo Polje, which I think was 14 -- 1389 and which is the defining event in their history, so I wrote somewhere in this book or elsewhere -- and this is not to criticize them at all, but the Serbs are a people who live their history like no other people on earth. That's not to criticize them, it's just one of the interesting things about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact -- and do I apologise to both the Court and counsel. Mr. Mair has just suggested to me that it might be helpful to mention that I'm referring to 1D 005556 when I'm referring to those pages in Mr. Bell's book, and to that extent I do apologise. If we could have that brought up generally. My apologies both to the Court as well as to you, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many 5s?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Three 5s and a 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the -- with regard to the self-same kind of idea, you also mention, and this is when you are referring to the Bosnian Serbs as opposed to any other group, I think, and this is page 113 of your book, sir, and that's page 12. You say: "... mostly their fierce isolation was self-imposed. They [were prisoners of their politics and their history, but I've sometimes wondered whether the mechanisms and dynamics of television may have also -- may also have had something to do with it. "Throughout the war we did not flit around evenly between one side and the other. Mostly, though I tried to break the habit, we did not flit at all. We stayed on the government side of the lines and reported from that perspective. For the kind of TV news operation that we were mounting is not a free running enterprise, it has a certain centre of gravity, and that is hard to move." First of all when you are dealing with the issue of their fierce isolation, I take it by that you are referring to characters, and I use the term in a loose sense for the moment, such as Karadzic? Or are you referring to just the people in general?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think I think both, sir. I mean obviously I got to know many of soldiers, civilians, at all levels, including what was at one time a sort of peace movement within the Bosnian/Serb army led by Major Mauzer from Bijeljina. So it wasn't just the leadership. I mean, I knew and I liked a lot of these people but I felt there was -- that they're so easily set in a sense of paranoia that the world was against them. And the reason I wrote that was machinery was much more primitive than it is now so we would be camped around a satellite dish, and the satellite dish started in Serb territory but then it migrated. And it was -- you know, to reach the Serbs once the war had started, you had to cross an active frontline. You might get shot at across the -- crossing the airport, so there was every reason to confine yourselves to government-held territory. Well, I got badly shot up once crossing the runway, but I still tried after that, and it was only in August 1994 that the Bosnian Serb territory was closed off to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. So up until August of 1994, and I not only do I understand why you may not wish to travel but it makes eminently good sense to me, and as a matter of fact, I take it that's one of the reasons that you created the Sarajevo corps was, as you said earlier, to protect lives as opposed to be recklessly out there trying to grab bits of sensational news. But considering that you have this understanding of them that they were prisoners of their politics and their history, with regard to the issue of the television reporting that was going on from a standpoint of what I'm going to call for a moment, if it makes sense, their isolation, did you ever get any sense that they believed that the information that was coming across the television was propaganda and was not to be believed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Some of them certainly believed this. One of the first things they did was to set up their own television service which they did with the help of some editing machines that they hijacked from the BBC, actually. So they could put out their own version of events.
