But even as late as August 1994, they had us over, there was a referendum on the, what was called the contact group plan, and we were led around the trenches and we were invited to interview anybody we liked. And the purpose of this was to show that the Bosnian Serbs were unanimously against the contact group plan. So they continued to deal with us up until that time. And I found if you had a reputation for being, the word the soldiers liked to use was "correct," they thought you were correct you could still do business with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And they thought you were correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Mostly they thought I was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's my understanding. And when you use this term "correct," actually, this is something that you've discussed in some previous testimony at some point. Could you explain to us what that term means? And from the standpoint of the Serbian interpretation of what it means to be correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The Serbian interpretation of being correct is this is a man who is reporting facts as he finds them and as he knows them and he is not coming to see us with a preconceived notion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, early on you met with a gentleman who said that the BBC was a Ustasha organisation, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Ustasha, yeah. Thank you very much. Did that view find voice in those Serb that you spoke with?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: If I remember, and you have the book in front of you and I don't, I think it was the commander of a Serbian artillery battery laying down fire on the frontlines. And I had to convince him that I was not Ustasha which is to say a Croatian Fascist, and he was, in the end, most forthcoming and gave me a wonderful insight into the Serbian mindset of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm -- another point you mention, and this is at page 109, and it's -- incidentally your memory is spot on. This is page 109, and it's page 11 of the document. You are talking about after a point that Milosevic had travelled to Pale to urge the Bosnian Serb parliament to ratify the plan. And further on that page you say: "Those who could dispersed to Belgrade and the rest returned to the trenches. The Serbs closed their ranks against the outside world of which we, in the press, were the most visible and intrusive symbol, so they set about curbing the intrusions." And then you explain that access became more difficult and a series of other things became increasingly hard from the standpoint of being able to deal with them. And I think one of the things that happens in both in a courtroom, as well as other places is the things are drawn in black and white, which obviously is not only inaccurate but also a bit naive. But with regard to the issue of, once again, the perception that the Serbs, and for the moment it's the Bosnian Serbs, had with regard to the reporting that was going on, did you ever get a sense from them that they didn't trust it? And by that I meant, the images that were being put forth?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: They certainly believed that the Bosnian government side were waging a propaganda war. As they closed off their frontlines so we couldn't get to them anymore, the only journalists in Pale with one or two exceptions were -- would be Serbs or Greeks or Russians, people of the Orthodox religion. And it was just impossible for us to report accurately what was going on except what we could see from their television service. For instance, the first we knew of the kidnapping of a military -- UN military observers in May 1995 was when we saw it on our screens. So that's what we were -- that's what we were reduced to. We didn't have the personal experience of talking to Karadzic, talking to Mladic. And I think our reporting obviously suffered from that. I wouldn't say it was biased, but it wasn't as -- we didn't have the same freedom at the end of the war that we had at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned at one point in your book, and you state -- and this is page 139, which is 20 in the e-court: "The satellite is as much a weapon of war as is the snipers rifle, and the sound bite is extension of warfare by other means. A modern-day Machiavelli or Klausewitz instead of conceding those to his adversary will co-opt them for himself."

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the modern military thinkers, people like General Sir Rupert Smith, have written intensively -- extensively on the importance of the information campaign. I mean you can -- you can win militarily, but lose politically and that's been the fact ever since Vietnam, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think we could agree that Vietnam was the first time that the military understood in a very particular sense the power of the media?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I would accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah. It stopped the war and brought down a president ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, well, I mean having said that, the first of our great war correspondents William Howard Russell from the Crimea, brought down a government in 1855 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: -- so there is a history.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And part of the importance of that history is to be able to accurately and dispassionately present to whatever the population is whether it be viewing or reading population, the circumstances that are surrounding the political and military will of the state that is waging the war?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah. I want to turn for a minute to the issue of UNPROFOR. And in your book you talk about "mission creep," but before we get to the issue of mission creep, which I understand to be defined as being given essentially a loose mandate and ultimately the activities on the ground evolve the purpose of what the people are there for. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I'd put it slightly differently. That a peacekeeping force becomes deployed and by the time it gets on the ground, the situation facing it has changed in such a way that it has either not to fulfill the mission or to redefine the mission as it goes along.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the presence of UNPROFOR, would you agree with me that its mandate was that, in the first instance, of peacekeeping, as opposed to peacemaking?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. Except that there was always the ambiguity of its name. The UN Protection Force which suggested that parts of its mission was do some protecting and by the time it arrived, it was a force of peacekeepers in a country where there was no peace to keep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So it was in an anomalous position because it had a mandate that it could not perform?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I quote one of its spokesman in the book, Alexander Ivanko, something to the effect was that we would love to do our mission if only someone in New York could explain to us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during the period of time that you were in the region, did you ever see that New York did explain to New York what its mission and by "its" I mean UNPROFOR's mission was?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Did they explain to UNPROFOR? Not in any coherent way. Both the British generals who commanded UNPROFOR in Sarajevo found this deeply contradictory. And in the end, General Smith got permission essentially to change the rules because the old rules were unworkable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to UNPROFOR, we heard yesterday some testimony with regard to the black-market transfer of fuel and foods, which is something that I believe you also were aware of. I'm not saying privy to, but you were aware of that, and you, as a matter of fact, discuss specifically the, I believe it was the Ukrainian unit that was involved in black-marketing fuel and other goods. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. The UNPROFOR was a force of very -- of national contingents of very different abilities, but I mean, there was never any suggestion of wrong-doing in that respect made against, shall we say, the British, the French or the Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. Do you know if the information, this is obviously something in your capacity as a reporter, the information that UNPROFOR units, certainly not the British, the French or the Dutch, but that UNPROFOR units were engaged in black-market smuggling with individuals in the area was a topic of discussion with the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was aware of this -- these allegations only at secondhand because for most of this phase of the war, I was out of Sarajevo and based in central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware of a particular protest by Mladic with regard to an UNPROFOR vehicle being used for moving weapons from one area of the region to another?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, sir. He may well have made the protest, but I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since I've mentioned General Mladic, I want to know whether or not -- well, I don't want to know whether or not. You state that Mladic was a maverick who accepted the political instructions that suited him and disregarded the rest.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I would add also, with respect, sir, that he was, which is not always the case with generals, he was widely admired by the soldiers under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I mean, he was a soldier's soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He was on the line, he was on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Sure. He was out, he was out with them a lot. He was not an armchair general.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: More like Patton and some of the others?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I've declared -- I've compared him once to General Schwarzkopf, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Gotcha. Now, with regard to this issue, which is that he accepted the political instructions that suited him and disregard the rest, during your time in the region did you perceive that there were equal powers between the military and the political arm, or that Mladic was under the command of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was aware of tensions between them. One of my friends was a British army major who was the liaison officer at Pale, the Bosnian Serbs headquarters, and I became aware in the later phases of the war that these tensions increased, especially after Dr. Karadzic started wearing a military uniform. And I quote somewhere in the book Karadzic regretting that they perhaps had made too much of a hero out of Mladic, so there were some serious, serious differences of opinion towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you in your capacity as a reporter determine whether or not when Karadzic rendered any orders, Mladic followed them or not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I don't think it was that kind of relationship, with respect, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Mladic would sit in on a lot of the important meetings with the mediators, but I would doubt very much if he regarded himself, Mladic, as an implementer of political decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: His position, I believe, is best voiced by his statement that history will judge him, which I'm sure it will, but --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, this was his reason for not dealing with the press. He said something like, I don't care about the press because I will be judged by history.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the structure of the dissemination of the information that was compiled, I'd like to see if I can get a clear understanding of that for myself, and perhaps for the Chamber and perhaps I'm the only one that is a bit confused here. The information when it first, and I'm talking about -- let's say, shall we split this up in terms of the way that the information was obtained, between the first period of time up to 1993 and then thereafter; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the first period of time when information was obtained, where did that information go? Physically, what happened to the clips, the footage?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The footage would be taken all around the city and to some extent all around the country. It would be assembled either initially in the hotel in Ilidza where we were and later in our offices in the television station. Because there was a pool, a lot of it would be traded, so you could have a report from Sarajevo at any time there and it might be the agency cameraman, your own cameraman, it might come from the French, it might come from the Germans, but obviously I would put a premium on what I had been present at myself and could witness personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, once you had the clip -- I'm sorry. Once you had the information in terms of the visual image, was that then sent out of the region?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. These images -- I mean, there are two sorts of information; there's the image and there's the facts. And it's the job of the reporter to assemble them and put them together in a coherent way and we -- ever since the arrival of the light hand-held camera in the early 1980s, we did our editing on site. One of our satellite dishes actually had a sniper's bullet through it, it was that close, and this gave us a wonderful freedom. Therefore you didn't have somebody calling you on your mobile phone and telling what you the feeling of the editorial meeting was in London. It was very direct and personal, and I did a lot of patrolling. I just went around the city seeing what I could find, which is -- you can't do that these days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No. When you had a completed, what I'll call product or completed story, that would be sent where?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It would be sent to my -- to the BBC in London. They had main television bulletins at 1 p.m., 6 p.m., and 9 p.m. So at ten to 1, ten to 6, and ten to 9, they would see this piece for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the other members of the reporting staff, I take it that what they were doing was something different than from what you were doing, by that I mean that you were not being sent to all of the television stations around the world, they had their own reporters?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: They had their own reporters. The French guy was particularly impressive. Some of the others tended to, to my mind, they spent too much time in bunkers, and also, to my mind, not enough of them tried to seek out the Serbs. Because I always felt that the Serbs held the key to this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to some of your colleagues, I believe that you mentioned that one of your colleagues -- or is it true that one of your colleagues did a fair amount of his reporting or her reporting, but I think it's a he, from the presidency?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That was in the early weeks of the war, that was John Burns of the New York Times whom I regard as a -- actually as a very good reporter, but he had some excellent sources inside the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, as you sit here -- as you sat there then, could you tell us what the, if you could, the psychological effect would be on people viewing, specifically the Serbs viewing such reporting coming from the presidency with regard to the issue of bias?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, for a start, they wouldn't have the sort of access to newspaper reports that they had to television reports, which came back to them. And I would go on to say in defence of Mr. Burns, that he also sought out the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not being critical of Mr. Burns whatsoever, it's really -- it's really because we understand that the true power of the image that is translated in television, and which is what I'm really driving at here. I mean, to see a reporter at the presidency building reporting would -- in a war where there are clearly two sides would lead one to believe that there was a concern about at least this international reporter if not many international reporters having a bias against the Serbs. That's what I'm asking you. If it's accurate, that's fine; and if it's not accurate, that's also fine, because I think you're in a better position to tell us than not.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: With respect, sir, I don't think it is accurate because the image of a newspaper reporter is not beamed around the world. His words are. It is the image of the television reporter who is beamed around the world. And if I had done my three and a half years inside and outside the presidency then I might well have been perceived to be biased, but this was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you discuss the issue of -- well, you state that the corruption of language, you talk about corruption of language and corruption of thought, which is obviously something comes out of a book. With regard to the issue here of the corruption of language and corruption of thought, in terms of the choice of words that were used, and I'm not talking about you in specific, but as a general proposition, considering some of the subjects we've talked about in terms of the use of the media by the respective parties, do you think it would be fair to say that by virtue of what -- we could call it David and Goliath kind of presentation by the media that there was in fact at a presentation level a corruption of language and thought?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, my words were always very low-key, and one of the arts of television is it shows things. You drop the adjectives, you drop the adverbs, the pictures are so powerful. So I think newspaper reporting and television reporting are completely different in that respect. I was at one time accused of, I think by the British foreign secretary, of being a founder member of the something-must-be-done club on Bosnia. I never campaigned for -- for this or that action because I didn't need to because the pictures made the case for me. That's not biased, that's as best you can showing things as they are, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the power of image and the choice of image, obviously that would influence the viewer, independent of -- independent of the accuracy or inaccuracy, you would agree, would you not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the repetition of image would also have that same effect?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is it fair to say there came a point in time in your thinking with regard to the entire issue of reporting that you made a determination to accept that the old BBC habits of distance and detachment were casualties and that, in fact, although you never, shall we say, verbally argued for, you made a determination that something was to be done and you proceeded, as did some of your colleagues, to go about doing that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: This is very interesting ground. I came to the conclusion that a reporter can be impartial or fair, but not between the armed and the unarmed, between the aggressor and the victim. For instance, some of the most powerful images in those years I got on the Bosnian Serb side of the lines in Grbavica where people hung carpets and sheets on wires across the road to blind the snipers on the other side. So it wasn't to that extent sort of one-sided. I was able to show that Serbs also were being sniped at and I think that was very important part of the story. But I was also very critical of the media towards the end of the war, I felt the whole thing was being reported from a corridor, perhaps 2 miles long, of the main road down the centre of Sarajevo. The worst casualties in the whole thing were in Tuzla in May 1995, where nearly 90 people were killed in a single bombing and that got hardly any coverage at all. Hardly any. And I was and remain very critical of some of our practices.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it that you do from what I've read and what I've heard you say in some speeches. I'd like to, if I could, for a moment shift gears because I've been alerted to something with regard to P 515.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we, first of all, have P 515 pulled up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we go to P 515, what do you want us to do with 05556?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Nothing at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I just wanted you to take a look at this image just for a moment, okay? And now what I'm going to do, just so you've seen it, you've indicated a couple of things among others, parts of it may be inexact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now what I would like to do is if I could, please, have the map that we used -- is there the ability to increase this now or is it still in the same position that we can't increase it? If we could just enlarge the area right around where it says "VRS." Can we make that any bigger?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know if that is of any help to you. Looking at this particular area and specifically going to where there are those black boxes below the V, what I'm wondering is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And now if we could make it smaller again just for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recognise that area as also being part of the ABiH territory?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, this is -- we are at now the Lukavica end of the runway and that was held by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned during your direct testimony, Mr. Bell, that some units of the BiH were billeted in schools. Do you have a recollection of how many units were billeted in schools?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: My only experience of this was when I, as I explained, I went to do a report about the Bosnian BiH Army training to break out of the siege and the unit, we went and found them in a school, that's it. But for the rest of it, I think there must have been sort of billeted among the people. I mean, it was not -- for much the war this was not a formed army and professional force like the -- as the Serbs had, though they formed themselves and trained themselves and became professional in the course of the war. It was very loose-knit. I mean, the Serbs never respected a lot of them because they wore trainers, if you would believe that. I mean, they didn't have boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That meant they weren't correct soldiers or they weren't soldiers at all?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yeah, we are going back to the definition of correct, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. I see, yes. So --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: But of course they were underestimated at the Serb's peril, because they were very good snipers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go back to 1D 005556 for but a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In your book you make the following statement which is that one of the lessons that's learned in peacekeeping is that all threats will be tested.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to your experience in the war here, would it be fair to say that a number of the threats that were made by the United Nations were not only tested, but upon them being tested, the United Nations was found wanting in delivering that which they had threatened?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I think this was especially the case in 1994 of the -- what we now see as the pin-prick -- pin-prick attacks in response to breaches of the cease-fire or movements of the -- of heavy weapons. It was only -- it was only in the late summer of 1995 that General Smith correctly assessed the forces, the balance of forces, what he had and what the Bosnian Serbs had, and he was able to take advantage of the -- his -- the UNPROFOR commander in Zagreb was on holiday, it was one of his children's weddings, and General Smith could then turn the key and use effective force which essentially changed everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in so doing, what he effectively did is he changed the policy because he had command for a day in the sense that the other gentleman was no longer in the seat of control, so he was able to take control?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: With the permission of New York. It was not a maverick decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That I understand. You mention also in your book that television by its very nature has an aptitude for illusion anyway and that reality is somehow diminished by being framed in the modest rectangle in the corner of living-room. And to the extent that we are dealing with an image that is being shot across the world, to what extent, if you have any thoughts about this being in the business of reporting for some many years now, to what extent does what your reality is on the ground understood by those that are watching it through the box?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I have written extensively about this. I've sometimes come out of scenes I was in, whether from Vukovar or Tuzla or Sarajevo or -- and you bring them back and you edit them and you think, Is that all there was, because you don't have the smell, you don't have the scene going on all around you. And there was another element that I also get into that we were forced by timid editorial decisions to take out nearly all the bloodshed because we didn't want to upset people, and this had the effect of sanitizing and actually, I would say, falsifying some of the coverage, but I fought this battle with my editors for many years and I lost it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Pity.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It is a pity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I want to get an understanding of something you said earlier on which is when you said trainers, I --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I mean shoes, I mean soft shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah. Because sometimes trainers are the --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, I mean the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Soft shoes.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I mean you are going to war in basketball shoes. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We see that happening increasingly throughout the world these days, do we not? Basketball shoes or bare foot, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Absolutely, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you think that in a certain sense, and I'm asking this based upon the experience you've had for all these years, that this war, and I hate to use the term, but this war was the first of the new wars that we are going to see and that as a result of it being a new war, all responses to it were at best confused?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, this is what General Smith now describes as war among the people. And the Iraq war was war among the people, what happened in Gaza was war among the people. The last time there was a set-piece tank battle was 1973, so we are out of the phase of industrial war into a different sort of war and the Bosnian conflict, what, 97.000 dead, was definitely one of those sorts of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that situation, once again based upon your experience, I take it that there's a fair amount of, I used the word before, confusion, but I'll use a different word which is there is a lack of clarity in terms of how these wars are going to be waged. I'm not referring to the rightness or the wrongness of it, but rather because we are dealing with a series of factors that we heretofore have not dealt with before, that internally there now are issues that have not been raised before, that we are for the first time having to address?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think that's a fair comment. The old cliche about the -- the old phrase the fog of war comes to mind here, with another new element that we haven't really had time to get into here which is the dissemination of atrocity stories, whether true or false, and the responsibility on the journalist not to go with secondhand information. That is, I was again and again told about this or that atrocity and I said, Show me, and they would say, No, sorry, the road is mined, we can't take you. And I just -- I would never report it because that can do so much damage and it did. People --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People believing the worst of another ethnic group and sometimes these prophecies become self-fulfilling, so I think that in this new kind of war there is an added obligation on the journalists to get their facts right and to be very, very careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to this war, if you were to give a grade to, I am not asking for to you give a grade to yourself, but a grade to the journalists that were involved in this new experience which had many factors that had heretofore not been addressed, understanding that's the case, do you think that they came up to the grade?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think I'd give the best an Alpha minus because, you know, we all make mistakes and some I wouldn't rate at all, honestly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have but a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have to confer with those that know better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I know the feeling, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your time, Mr. Bell. I really do appreciate it and I'm once again thankful for your candour and your thoughtfulness, and I mean that in a very sincere fashion.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, you were asked a series of questions, in fact there was a lot of discussion about the part that the media had to play in depicting the war and also guiding the various decisions that were made by the parties concerned. And you also spoke in your evidence about meetings and access you had to political and military authorities involved in the conflict. What I want to ask you is whether you got a sense of whether those authorities were aware of the role that the media might potentially play in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they were. They were very keen on getting their point of view across in the world media. And there was another unusual dimension to this, that if they were involved in sensitive negotiations over a prisoner exchange or a body exchange, they would actually ask for the international media to be present because they felt that in the presence of television cameras from the outside world, it would make the other party more likely to honour the obligations it had entered into. So quite -- I think actually without intending to we may even have done a little bit of good in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Did you get a sense whether the political and military authorities were themselves paying attention to what was being reported?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think they were. The -- some of the military commanders would actually have their own -- their own cameramen with them, it was part of the old Yugoslav way and some of the most vivid pictures we received in the whole war came from a young man who was the cameraman of Colonel Ruskic [phoen] who was -- appeared before this court, so there were many different sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Was this a feature of what was happening at the end of the war or was there -- this awareness of the power of the media, if you like, from 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think by the time, by 1995 all parties to the conflict had become acutely aware of the power of the media, and that is why we found ourselves increasingly hemmed in and restricted as time went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Are you able to give us your indication as somebody who was there throughout the period as to a particular point in time where people started realising the potential power of the media in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think it was probably after the ending of the side war between Muslims and Croats which ended in February 1994, and then we faced a war -- apparently a war without end between the Muslim Croat Federation on one side and the Bosnian Serbs on the other. And as I became increasingly aware of the weakness of the Bosnian Serbs in manpower, but of course I couldn't -- by then I couldn't get -- have the personal touch I had earlier, and I found that on the BiH side, the roadblocks were going up all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, thank you. That's all I have for you. Their Honours may have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, with the Chamber's indulgence and my colleagues, I forgot to ask Mr. Bell one question. If I could be permitted to do so. It does not cover anything that Mr. Thomas has just discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour, provided if there's any issue arising, I be afforded the same opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the courtesy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I do apologise to you, I've been through your book so many times and noted different things that I just forgot this. You said in your book, and I'm going back to this one issue, this is on -- it's page 114, which would be 13 of 1D 005556. I'm reading from the middle of the paragraph: "In this self-critical mode, I would ask myself when had we ever shown a civilian victim of sniper fire on the Serb side of the lines, when had we reported from their hospitals, when had we heard from the Sarajevo Serbian news in Grbavica rather than Oslobodjenje" -- did I pronounce it properly?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "Oslobodjenje, the celebrated newspaper on the government side which was an icon of journalism and a symbol of the city's ordeal." And my question to you is with regard to the newspaper and the government side, when did Oslobodjenje start becoming a newspaper on the government side?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, it was Sarajevo's daily newspaper, but after the war started the Serbs then published their own version of Oslobodjenje which was actually edited by a friend of mine. So there were two rival versions of Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the Oslobodjenje that you are refer to here that is the Oslobodjenje of the ABiH side, to put it in those terms?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yeah, it's headquarters were ruined, it was one of the iconic images ever the war, the state of its headquarters. But I'm being critical of my own profession there, but that's one of my failings, I question a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I certainly find no fault in the work that you've done. I think many that have seen what you've done find absolutely no fault in it either, sir, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Nothing, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we proceed, may the record show that we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis during this session as Judge David had to be absent for reasons beyond his control, and Judge Picard is sitting on my left simply because her desk is -- she is locked in that side and her papers are on that side. You had finished. Do you have any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, I've got just two questions for you. The first one is: On which side of the war was Haris Silajdzic and what was his position?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: He was at that time the prime minister of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so he was on the government side of the lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And at page 61 of the transcript, starting from line 1, you were asked a question that -- well, it was put to you that "... amongst others we are dealing with a series of factors that we heretofore have not dealt with," and you quickly answered to say, "I think that's a fair comment." What factors are these that you are dealing with at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: There are two that come to my mind immediately, Your Honour. One is the power of the medium of the media and especially of television to shape the response of governments, especially when they do not have a settled policy. It's been described once as the CNN factor, I believe. So this imposes an extra responsibility on the journalists involved. And the other is the nature of the war, the -- that this was not an old-fashioned war, although the weapons were old-fashioned, it was a war among the people in which the suffering of civilians was so evident that the suffering of civilians also to some extent shaped the world's reactions and I think required governments to respond finally, although they were very slow to do it in a way that they wouldn't have been obliged to in a less media-driven age. I think that those are the new elements, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions arising from the questions by the Bench, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: No sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: None, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mr. Bell. This concludes your testimony and let me take the time to say thank you for taking the time off your busy schedule to come and testify at the Tribunal. You are now excused. You may stand down and please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Ms. Bolton will lead the next witness. That concludes my business before you, and that of Mr. Cannata this afternoon, if we could please be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good evening, Your Honours. The next witness for the Prosecution will be Mesud Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mesud Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: He is a 92 ter witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, could you begin by stating your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I am Mesud Jusufovic. 17th of February, 1960.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that on the 3rd of April, 2002, you had occasion to testify in the matter of Prosecutor v. Stanislav Galic?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And yesterday you had occasion or the opportunity to listen to the recording of your testimony, an audio recording of your testimony in those proceedings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry. I think I had my headphones on the wrong channel and I didn't hear the response to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What channel are you on?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now I'm on channel 4, is that the correct channel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the correct channel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. And was the recording that you listened to yesterday in a language that you understood?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in my language.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And were the answers that you provided in that previous testimony true and correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of the answers were correct and true and I stand -- I remain by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I asked you those same questions today, would you answer them in the same manner?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I should point out one thing, and that is that when you were questioned the last time, back in 2002, about your occupation, at that time you were the commander of the professional fire brigade in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you've since been promoted?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, within the last six months I became the civil defence secretary within the canton of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And with the exception, then, of that area of your testimony being different, was the remainder of your testimony from 2002 still correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I wonder if, Madam Registrar, if you could please bring up 65 ter 09412. Your Honours, that is an official transcript of the audio recording that the witness listened to yesterday, and it has been redacted to indicated the portions of the transcript that the Prosecution is seeking to have filed pursuant to 92 ter and I would ask that it be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. And it may be so marked, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P520.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And with the Court's permission, Your Honours, I have a few clarifying questions I'd like to ask and then a brief summary of the witness's evidence I'd like to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very few indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Very few, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, during your previous testimony in the Galic matter, you had indicated that there were many buildings and monuments that were set ablaze by Bosnian Serb army shells during the conflicts; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, if you could bring up 65 ter 03061, please. There should also be an English translation of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness if you recognise the document that's in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The only thing being that there is no English version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I have the ERN number, pardon me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I am informed that there's a problem in that the English version doesn't seem to be appearing. If I could proceed with the questioning of the witness, I think it will become quite clear what the document is and perhaps we could find the English version at a later point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who authored this document?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: This is the record that we have in our fire brigade on the computer and when I needed this for the purposes of this court then we just printed this list showing all facilities that had been shelled. I think that I signed it, that my signature is on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could actually go to the third page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in terms of the kind of facilities, there's 120 names listed of facilities, did you include every single place in Sarajevo that there was a fire at?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, not all of the locations. Only the more important facilities and locations that were shelled and set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what time-period does this document cover, sir?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: This document pertains to the period from the 5th of April, 1992, until the 10th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And were there any fires as a result of shells at public buildings that post-dated August 10th, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Naturally there were. Throughout the war civilian facilities were shelled, especially cultural and historical monuments, as well as buildings where people resided in large numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I wonder if this item could be marked as the next Prosecution exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. May it please be so marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P521.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: A few more questions, sir. One of the things you indicated in the Galic proceeding was that there were approximately 67 Serbian members of the fire brigade that left just prior to the outbreak of hostilities. I'm wondering if you could tell me if they left of their own volition or if they were terminated?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Based on my conversations with these people, because not all of them had left, 67 firefighters of Serb ethnicity left whereas 10 of them remained, they to me confirmed that they had a meeting with Radovan Karadzic and that he had instructed them to leave Sarajevo, and they simply didn't show up for work one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Another issue that you discussed in your testimony, sir, was the fact that there was a number of members of your brigade who were killed or injured during the war, and I just wondered if you had a total count of the number of firefighters who were killed during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict 12 firefighters were killed and 58 of them were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And of the 12 that were killed, how many were killed while on duty?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Three were killed on duty. Two while putting out fires, and one was killed while he was repairing the fire engine within our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And for those three people, what was the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The cause of death was a shell. If you wish, I can give more details.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We'll just deal with the total numbers for now, sir. Turning to the people who were wounded, how many of those firefighters were wounded in the course of duty?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Thirty-eight were killed while on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, you just said killed, I thought we were talking about wounded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At least that is what the interpretation said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't hear your comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At least that is what the interpretation came across as. I don't know whether the witness had said killed, but the interpretation said killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My friend is shaking his head and I think it was an interpretation error, that you actually said wounded, and I just want to clarify. We are talking about people who were wounded, not killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I said wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So 38 of the 58 were wounded on duty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Out of those 38, there are those who had been wounded on a number of occasions. I, for example, was wounded twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And with respect to those 38 including yourself, what were the causes of the wounds?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The cause of the wounds were always the shells. When we went out to put out fires, they would increase the shelling of the area where we were putting out fires. In Sarajevo, the most dangerous situations were when there was a location on fire. All the citizens fled from there because they knew that the people from the hills would fire at the firefighters, and that this is why it was so dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What do you mean by people from the hills?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, were any of those 38 firefighters who were injured while on duty acting in a military capacity at the time?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No. Within the fire brigade there were no members of the army. There couldn't have been any because we worked almost continuously. Most of the firefighters remained within the fire brigade because it was a major problem to come to work and to go home from work without falling casualty to shelling. That is to say, that none of the firefighters were members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The last thing I want to ask you about, sir, is in your previous testimony you spoke about attending fires in hundreds of buildings and you told the Court in those proceedings that with the exception of responding to fires at the Tito barracks, where UNPROFOR soldiers were stationed, that you saw no evidence of any of these buildings being used for military purposes. And I want to clarify whether you personally attended all of the fires you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't have been at all fires. It was physically impossible. There were situations where there were 15 fires simultaneously at different places. Mostly fires were set up by incendiary rounds, mostly in areas where there were monuments or where people resided. If people had nowhere to reside, they had to leave Sarajevo. That is to say, that all of those were civilian facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So in cases where you couldn't personally attend the fires, what's the source of your information that these weren't military installations?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Out of the firefighters -- or, rather, from the firefighters who went out to work, we would get reports. It is possible that sometimes there were some military facilities because we firefighters do not pay attention to what is on fire. We go out to put out fires. I, myself, always went only to fires where there were civilian facilities burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just with respect to the list that you have already identified for us, Prosecution Exhibit 520, were you aware of any of those facilities being used -- sorry, 521. Were you aware of any of those facilities being used for military purposes at the time of the shellings?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what I know, no. I came to the fire brigade about the 20th of June, 1992. From that time on, I don't know of any cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At this juncture, with the Court's permission, I'd just like to read a brief summary of this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In 1992, Mr. Jusufovic was the third highest ranking member of the Sarajevo fire brigade. His superiors included a man named Radomir Spaic who was a Serbian gentleman. Commencing in early 1992, Mr. Spaic ordered the transfer of much of the forces equipment to Pale, which was an area controlled by Bosnian Serbs. That included the transfer of fire trucks, radio equipment, fuel, as well as other equipment. By the time the shelling of Sarajevo commenced in April 1992, the Sarajevo fire department had only 14 vehicles, little fuel, and no spare parts. In addition, there were 67 Serbian members of the fire brigade who left the force just prior to the outbreak of the hostilities, taking additional equipment with them. The VRS forces used both ordinary shells and incendiary shells containing phosphorus. Even non-incendiary shells often sparked fires. Fires were a daily occurrence and the firefighters were constantly busy. The VRS targeted all kinds of buildings in Sarajevo including apartment buildings, schools and hospitals, as well as food and waterlines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, please. The stenographer can't keep pace with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Certainly. Immediately prior to shelling a monument or building, the VRS would typically shell the fire stations. And the witness presumes that the VRS was endeavouring to prevent the fire brigade from responding to the fire. Firefighters were routinely fired at by snipers and targeted by shells, both while they were en route to fires and while they were fighting fires. To avoid being hit by shells or snipers, members of the fire brigade learned to park their vehicles in locations where they would be sheltered from incoming explosives. They learned not to enter buildings through the doors, but instead to make holes in the walls and enter the buildings through those holes. They learned to crawl by windows inside the building to avoid sniper fire. And despite these tactics, many fire fighters were wounded and some were killed by shells, grenades, and sniper fire. The brigade's ability to fight fire was compromised by the fact that the VRS controlled the electrical and water supplies. Frequently the only source of water was the well at the brewery, and fire trucks came under fire whenever they attended the brewery to refill their tanks. The professional brigade was assisted by volunteers, both the professional brigade and the volunteer societies were civilian organisations, neither had ties to the army or police. The brigade responded to fires in hundreds of buildings during the conflict, and the witness did not personally see nor did he hear of evidence that any of the buildings, with the exception of the Tito barracks, were being used for military purposes at the time. Those are all of my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you sit down, ma'am, in your reading of that statement, at the beginning you said at page 76, line 6: "Commencing in early 1992, Mr. Spaic ordered the transfer of much of the force's equipment to Pale." Which force is this?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This is the Sarajevo fire brigade's equipment being transferred to Pale area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that you, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Novak Lukic, I will be putting questions to you on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Perisic. You have experience in testifying before this Tribunal and you know that you need to wait -- I'm actually here to remind you that you need to wait after my question. You see, I'm being reprimanded by the Presiding Judge already, so please try to answer my questions slowly so that the transcript can be accurate, and interpretation as well. When the war started, and you said that that was sometime in April of 1992, you lived in Vratnik, and this is where you were based throughout the war. That's where you lived; correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time you and a group of citizens residing there organised yourselves within one month and you set up barricades and checkpoints in that neighbourhood in the area where you lived; correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not set up barricades, we dug out trenches near the barracks in Vratnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were the commander in that location?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: If one may call the leader of 30 to 40 people a commander, in that case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how was it that you became the commander? Who appointed you to that post?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of April, the shelling started and people started fleeing to their homes. Most of them came to the culture hall and those who were present concluded that we had to defend our families, our children, our wives because we had the previous experience in Croatia, and it was then that we decided that we had to organise ourselves to defend Vratnik, and there were 20 to 30 of us there and the people said that I should be the one leading the effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what were you doing at that time? What was your occupation? Were you already working as a firefighter then or not?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I've been a firefighter since 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, for awhile you were a taxi-driver?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: From 1980 until 1986 I was a taxi-driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo the whole time?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Sarajevo the whole time. I was born there and live there to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that already in March of 1992 barricades were set up and checkpoints throughout Sarajevo both by the members of the SDS party and by the members of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In March there were barricades, I know of them because my wife used to work in Grbavica and she couldn't go to her office. But I don't know that the SDA set up any barricades. I know only of the Serbian barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that the SDA members set up any barricades?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the army of BH was set up in April of 1992 on the basis of the decision of the presidency of BH?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible that there was a decision of the presidency, but there was no army at the time. There were only the units in existence, such as the unit that I was a member of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when did you become aware or, rather, when do you consider that the BH Army was set up and that it existed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the Territorial Defence, not yet the army at the time, but the Territorial Defence was set up sometime in late May or early June, as far as I can remember, because this is when I joined the fire brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened when you joined the fire brigade, when you rejoined the fire brigade, if I may refer to it so, what happened with your neighbours who also organised themselves, those 30 to 40 men, did they join the army?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: When the mobilisation order was issued, everyone had to be assigned to some unit. Most of these men were in the Territorial Defence which later became the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the presidency of the Bosnia-Herzegovina had declared a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that all men of military age had to be mobilised into some kind of unit or a work detail?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone had to be in some kind of unit, either in civilian protection or the army or the Territorial Defence, or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the forces which were loyal to the BH presidency in spring of 1992 took over the strategic vital facilities in Sarajevo, whereas the Serbs withdrew to the hills around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that BH Army members took up some positions. I know that before April the Yugoslav People's Army was busy digging in the tanks and building up positions around Sarajevo. This we could see on TV. And when people ask what this was, Kukanjac explained -- or, rather, I'm not sure if it was Kukanjac or someone else, but somebody said that they were protecting these positions from an external enemy. And then later on, they used this as positions from which they shelled Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your evidence in the Galic case, on page 6522, line 9, you said, and this was redacted later or, rather, it was changed, altered, it did not enter into this portion of the transcript, so I'd like to refresh your memory. Line 9, I will read this in English, you said: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... who had left they have also shelled us and they have also shelled our fire station." [Interpretation] And then after this, in answer to Judge Orie's question, on page 6524, line 25, you said that you meant that they actually joined and fought as members of the Serbian army but not that they specifically shelled you.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think what I meant was that they had joined the Serbian side, but the reason why I thought they were shelling us was because they would advise us in advance. They would tell us -- they would call the station and say, Now your -- a shell is coming your way, and then they would announce, Five more shells are going to land on your station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, but in any case from what you've said here and the portion that you've corrected, there is no reason for to you believe that they were personally trying to shell you?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, were all the hills -- were all the positions on the hills around Sarajevo held by the members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know many of these positions, but I know that members of the BH Army were on Trebevic, on Brijeg, then I think on Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, let me be more specific, do you know who held the Zuc hill?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I think the Zuc hill was held by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Mount Igman, if I remember this correctly, I think there was some movements there of the army. There was the BH Army and then the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the BH Army had mortars?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: While I was there, we didn't have anything. We would observe from Lapusnica them shelling us, this was from about 800 metres, and we would just lie there because there was nothing we could shell them with or there was nothing we could shoot and reach them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, so when you say "when I was there," you mean when you organised yourself, but what I'm referring to is the period while you were a fireman, a firefighter. Up until the Dayton Accords, since you were in contact with many people and were -- attended many events, do you know or did you hear that the BH Army had mortars on the Sarajevo theatre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry. My friend began that question by assuming that in fact the witness was talking about the period of time when he was in the, I guess, neighbourhood defence and I think he should actually put that question to him. I don't know if that is what he's talking about or isn't, but I think the witness needs to clarify that, and my friend not to just assume that is the period of time he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that for you to clarify that in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's simply that I understood from the guide-lines that we were supposed to be asking succinct, sort of one question at a time and then moving on, so that was the basis for my objection. I can clarify it otherwise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suggest you do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness understood me and the portion where he was describing this particular time he was even nodding, so I didn't feel it was necessary to explain what period this was referring to. But let me go back to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember throughout the war period, did you have any information that the BH Army had some mortars in the Sarajevo theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot claim this with any certainty because I had no ties with the army because we were continuously busy putting out fires, so I really don't know. We were -- it's possible during the war that they acquired them, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear stories or see evidence that the BH Army had long-barrel weapons as well?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see this myself. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of stories of this?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that during the war in Sarajevo there were some 35.000 members of the BH Army in Sarajevo and about as many around Sarajevo on positions that were held by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what the figures were, but it's possible that there were as many.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you did not have any contact with the army. As firefighters, you belong to the civilian protection, if I understand you correctly, is this correct, the professional fire brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The professional fire brigade and all the volunteer firefighters, and there were five such societies in the town, they were under civilian protection and they were units of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have meetings with your superiors from the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have some official meetings with police members?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I think no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To be more precise, was there at any point in time during the war did you have any kind of meetings with the BH Army representatives?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not have any meetings with BH Army members. We only had meetings in the town hall where we were invited to come to meetings by the mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you recall if there were any army representatives there, any army members there?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me, no, because the army was not really into the civilian administration. They didn't really care for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 6533, in line 7, among the sites that were shelled, you also mention the Holiday Inn. You say that it was a very attractive target, and you also say on the same page, in line 23, that you had to attend or respond to fire calls from that position over 500 times, that's at least what you said, up until the summer of 1994. Can you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Holiday Inn was open as a hotel throughout the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The 500 fires until the summer of 1995 were so bad that -- and you were so successful in putting out those fires that the hotel remained open throughout the period?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, because we would be there on time. We were on the spot to put out the fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I would now like to show you Exhibit 521. Could we please pull it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First I'd like to ask you something about this document. You just mentioned that you printed this out from your database of the records that were kept for that period. My question is this: First of all to say what the title of this document is, Fires on High Profile Facilities. Could you please tell us what do you understand to mean -- or what do you understand is meant by high profile facilities? What was the criterion?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a facility where a lot of people lived or important cultural and historic monuments, significant for our people's history and tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please leaf through all these three pages and tell us whether these facilities are -- whether most of them are public buildings, not residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: From what I can see here there are no apartment buildings, no residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now put some questions about some of these individual facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 1 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under 3, it says the MUP motel. MUP stands for the Ministry of the Interior; correct? That's a police facility; correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, MUP means the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that was a police facility?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, that was a hotel owned by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Under 4, it says, MUP, the Vraca facility. Could you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: This is the police academy where -- police academy with cadets, so there was an attack on this school and a fire there. These cadets were young people between the ages of 14 and 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this was in early 1992, in the beginning of the conflict, right, on the 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under 18, we see it says, Magros Wholesaler Point. Is this a commercial facility?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Magros is a company. It is a commercial company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under 38, we see a Magros store. That is another commercial facility; correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they sold food there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under 27, I see that you mention the Holiday Inn on the 24th of May, 1992, and there is no further mention of the Holiday Inn 500 fires on this list. What is the reason?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The mention that was made here on the 24th of May, 1992, was because we actually went to the hotel from the fire brigade premises because we did not have a unit on the premises of the hotel itself. But because it was impossible to get to this hotel across Marin Dvor because it was being shelled all the time, we set up a unit in the basement of the Holiday Inn and we had fire hoses all around the hotel so that the fires were put out by the men who were stationed on the premises of the Holiday Inn. And that is why there is no further mention of it on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were these other fires also recorded in your database?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't. They were only logged in a log-book by the duty officers because we would respond -- we would record an intervention when a vehicle left our premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what is listed here are the fire events or fire incidents where you actually had to send fire trucks from the station?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And for those about 500 Holiday Inn fires, you have no records at your police -- at your fire station whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, we don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
